utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. We hope the technical problems that delayed the start have been overcome. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the affirmation and read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Now if you'll excuse me a minute, there is a matter that I want to attend to. Could I mention, Mr. Moore, that much time was spent in cross-examination and examination with the last witness over the transcript of the notes. I don't believe that that is in -- been exhibited. Is it something that you would wish to have exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If Your Honour forgive me, I misunderstand. Are you talking about the transcript that rolls through, or transcript in relation to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's my use of the word "transcript," my fault. The notes -- the typed version of the notes or diary kept by the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I thought they had been exhibited. If they have not, I will make an application for them to be exhibited. I would have thought in any event they would have to go in with the handwritten version, because that is the source of it. And some of that document is written in English. If they have not been exhibited, I would make an application for them to go in as A and B, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have that question clarified. You are suggesting to me they may have been exhibited as part of the exhibit which is the diary or the notes themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nor can I. It seemed to me, though, that they had not been. And I haven't marked my copy, which I usually would, if it had been exhibited. So we will have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we can come back to it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, might I just, if Your Honour has concluded on that, we have prepared a short bundle. The Court, I hope, has got a copy for this witness. It should say "Dr. Schou." There are a small number of tabs. What I have done is I have continued the tab numbering so that it flows from what I will call the Kypr tabs. So Ambassador Kypr, the bundle there, ran up, I think, to 37. Some of them, I think, were not exhibited. But they can always be deleted and removed. And these, then, continue on 38 through to 42 inclusive. The reason is, I hope, reasonably straightforward. They are in the same mission, and Dr. Schou may well be referred to some of the earlier documents or exhibits, and for assistance, if they are referred to by way of tab number, then we can go immediately to it rather than try and find out which is which. That's the first thing. The second is there is an index which the Court should have. The Court and my learned friends have got it in two pages, I've got it in three because of my failing eyesight, and that relates to all the exhibits that have already been placed before the Court. And then there is 65 ter numbers. To assist the administration, we have got the ERN numbers, you can see in red for court officer in the top right-hand corner, and the B/C/S version so if there is any difficulty, it's there. And then, finally, if I ask the Court, please, to turn to tab 42, this is not a document my learned friends have seen; indeed, I have not seen before last night. It is a Danish newspaper that was brought by the witness we did not have. The date is the 21st of November, and it relates to -- it is in Danish, it has not been translated for obvious reasons. And there is a part of it that I would seek to refer to. So that just, I hope, assists. The 21st of November document, the 42nd tab, relates to, to help my learned friend, that this doctor made a phone call to a journalist in Denmark saying that a number of people were missing from the hospital and that he was aware of it on that day. I see Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to express the position of the Defence. All three teams agree as for the latest document mentioned by Mr. Moore, we object to even discussing this document, first and foremost because we received it this morning in our lockers; hence, the dead-line of 24 hours had not been met. We were unable to run through the document, we were unable to check it, it's in Danish, and irrespective of the witness's ability to perhaps translate that a vista, this goes against our position and against the system used at this Tribunal, and it would go against the rules and the dead-lines set as for the disclosure to the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no problems with that at all. Can my learned friend please remove that document? I will not rely on the document itself, but I am perfectly entitled to ask this doctor what he actually did. The evidence will go in that way. If my learned friend wishes to helpfully approach the case in this way, then I will correspondingly do so. We will not rely on the document, but we will rely on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moore, if you are ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This again changes the usual practice. We have his statement, but we haven't been notified of this new information that the OTP learned while proofing the witness, and again we hear it for the first time, hence this presents a new OTP policy. Therefore, we are against posing questions on facts that we haven't been prior -- notified about before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As I have already said to my learned friend, I saw this document for the first time last night. If in actual fact my learned friend is going to be technical about it, I will not seek an adjournment, I will proceed with this evidence. He has got notice of it now, and I will make an application for an adjournment and call it first thing tomorrow morning, which is 24 hours notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, instead of firing off quickly, if you pause and allow the Chamber to intervene, it might make life less heated. We understand that a witness has come with an additional fact. It's something which helps the witness confirm a date, as I understand it. That being so, with leave of the Chamber you may lead the evidence. If that produces a problem for the Defence, that can be raised and we will consider that problem and how to deal with it. Not now, but when it happens you can then assess whether or not it produces a problem for you. If the Chamber didn't take that position, where there is a genuine case of something new coming when a witness arrives, from the Chamber's experience it would be in the long run of the trial more likely to harm the Defence than the Prosecution. Because we have experienced far more Defence witnesses arriving with additional information than the other way. And of course it depends on how critical the fresh information is. If it's fundamental, a very different issue arises. But if it's merely helping a witness confirm a date when some incidental issue occurred, we think it better to understand the humanity of the situation and ensure that the evidence is able to be led whether it be from Prosecution or Defence. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is your full name?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: My full name is Jan Allan Schou.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say you are actually -- you were born in 1955, you have that benefit?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The 10th of April, I think, is your date of birth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You are of Danish nationality?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with your personal circumstances and then move on to your professional. Is it right that you are a married man and you have three children?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I am not married any longer but I have three children, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That you are a Danish citizen, that you attended, as you describe it, grammar school, and you then attended the military academy, and that started in 1974?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer for the sake of interpreters and the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right it say that as a result of that you were able to study at the academy to become an army officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: After two years you then decided to leave the army. You had been a full-time soldier and you started, I think, at the university of Copenhagen?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it was there that you studied medicine?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, may I just deal in general terms, please, with your medical practice. I think it's right to say that as of today you have practiced as a surgeon and a gynaecologist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that is in Jutland --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- in Denmark itself? In relation to your military service, is it right that by 1991 you were a reservist?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think in 1991 you were actually requested by the Danish army, because of the qualifications that you had, both militarily and medically, you were requested to go to Yugoslavia, as it was then called, to attend as an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At that time is it right you were holding the rank of captain, and on the mission that you were sent you recollect that there were 14 personnel involved?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with it in, I hope, relatively briefly, you left Denmark on the 15th of October, 1991, and you eventually ended up in Zagreb in Croatia which was, as far as I can understand, the location that you were at was the ECMM headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I would like to commence, if I may, please, with the 18th of October. I think it's right to say then that you left Zagreb for Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, why was it that on the 18th of October you went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was because we have to follow the Medecins sans Frontieres to evacuate the -- some patient from the hospital. And we had to monitoring it as an ECMM member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what exactly was your function within the mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: My function was to -- as a special to monitoring the hospital. How it works, how the -- the patient were behaving, and what -- what they need, equipment, medical stuff and something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the mission that went to Vukovar, how many people actually went to Vukovar itself; could you remember?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure. I think we were four or five ECMM cars with three person in each.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I want to do is I'd like you, and I hope you've got this bundle, to turn to what we call tab 38. It's the supplementary bundle. The ERN number in English is 0036-6961 through to 71 and 0305-5390 through to 96. Now, have you got that tab, as we call it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I have got it. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So do I. It should say "Vukovar relief mission." And it should be a handwritten document, I think not in your -- in your writing.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No, it's not my writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But top left-hand corner should be 18th of October, depart Zagreb at 1400?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just deal, if we may, with one or two matters, but we will refer to this document in due course. I think it's right that you stopped at a place called Djakovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think that you slept there, and about 5.00 in the morning, as far as you can recollect, you left that place and drove through Nustar, then to Zidine, Marinci, and as far as I can understand, you arrived at Marinci at about 7.00 in the morning. Now, can we just look at the document that we have, document 38?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I see there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the beginning of the testimony I wanted to introduce an objection in principle. With the previous witness the policy was to go through the documents and it is a way of leading. But specifically in this case when Mr. Moore began his examination-in-chief, he read out to the witness that they spent the night in Djakovo. That's not in the document, but the witness confirmed nevertheless. Therefore, I wish that either stick with the documents, or perhaps ask the witness to provide his answer and not to lead in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, forgive me. The document says: "Arrive on the 18th of October at Djakovo at 2100." Then it shows the 19th of October "Depart Djakovo." And forgive me for being a little simple, I would have thought that in actual fact that would indicate that between the 18th and 19th, that they were located at that position and therefore stayed the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on as you are, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just move on, please. Can we deal then, please, from your memory, if it's possible, when you got to Marinci, I think it's right to say that the document suggests that it was ahead of schedule. Now, can I just deal with this document itself so everybody understands how this document -- where it comes from? Do you know who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It come from the -- the head of the -- you can say the chief of the relief mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we look at the document itself, bottom right-hand corner, 961962, 63, and continuing, there is a signature. Whose signature is that? Bottom right-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: You are saying about my signature in the -- in the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. It's when I -- when I give this -- this document to the -- to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We just have to establish the source of the document, and we now have that. Can we deal, then, please, with the route itself? And I want to deal with the entry where it says -- and you can see it on the document, the first page, that you remain on the road outside of Marinci until 7.55 when a JNA colonel arrived. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what happened there, please? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We -- we were stopped outside the city, I don't know for how long time, and then we went into Marinci. And our cars were controlled, there were no weapons in the cars. And then after a while we were sent forward to next city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you, please, to look at a document that is at the very end, or a page that's the very end of this document? Its number is 6971.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can you just tell us -- I don't know if it's possible for it to be shown in a way that is not upside down. Can that be done? There we are now. Now, dealing with the document, who drew this document; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It -- the document is made by the chief of this relief mission, which was a French ECMM member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When we look at it, is it right to say that it obviously the head is relief operation to Vukovar, 18th to the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what exactly does it show us in general terms, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: In general terms, it show us that we have to pass the no-man's land, I think, four times before we reached Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so when we look at it, we can see Vinkovci; then on the left-hand side Nustar; Zidine?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Zidine, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now we've got dotted lines and it seems to be -- under the subheading of JNA and Marinci, and we've got the time 7.10; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now what exactly does this signify, the dotted lines, which seem to be either side of Marinci?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's -- it's what I remember is that there were a check-point we had to pass to get into Marinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the dotted line coming out of Marinci?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's when we leave Marinci, then we go out, go out to a check-point again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: And it's -- it's what you call the front line of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now when we deal, if you just keep your thumb on that particular page and we move on, I think it's right to say that the document, if we look at the first page of document, 6961, the one I have referred you to, so try and keep your finger with the diagram, and 6961 is the English version, we've got: "Convoy proceed to eastern point to Marinci and stopped." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then we've got: "Lead EC vehicle, proceeds to Croat lines."

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it right that when we look at the map we can see that is represented on the diagram itself?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we've got the arrowed line going through to Bogdanovci to check the route and establish a contact. Can we turn over the page, please? I want to try and deal with this relatively briefly. We've got an entry, and I think it's right that the vehicle returns, it -- to use your phrase, it picks up the convoy, mines on approach. Can you deal with those, please, what had happened with the mines on approach.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It means that on the road there were mines and the Croatian forces put them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we just move on. There is the arrival at that particular location. The remainder there for 30 minutes. Now, what is it the -- the phrase "while local commander"? It seems to say "Croatian commander"; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what it says then and explain?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It says that in the city of Bogdanovci, the local commander of the Croatian force in that small village, which were almost surrounded by JNA, he was telling us that we couldn't go through this -- the normal way, which were in the agreement, because the road was mined. And they know a way to the hospital we could, travelling with an escort, with an -- with some of the Croats, so we can pass JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can I see if I've got this correct? The agreed route, you had been told by the Croat commander that you could not go that route because there were mines, but he knew another route that was not mined?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And so eventually team V, was that the team, as you called yourself? You see the next entry.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. "In Nustar inspects area and finds no mortars or artillery positions." Are you able to help us with regard to that entry or not? About "no mortars and no artillery positions."

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I saw nothing at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with -- with your brief? You clearly have a medical brief, but you had military training and you were contacted by the Danish military specifically because of your double expertise. Did you receive any briefing by the military prior to going on either mission or on this particular mission on the 18th, 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: On the 18th of the -- particularly the 18th of October we get -- I get nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: But when I left Denmark, I have a short meeting with -- with the Danish military that show us -- that said to us, to all the Danish monitors, that we have to go through Yugoslavia and that we of course had to watch the equipment they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you say about equipment, I am presuming one is not talking about bulldozers. Are we talking about military equipment?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why was it that it was of interest for military equipment to be looked at in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was because in the Danish army at that time we only had pictures of these vehicles they have, so it was first time we see it real. And we have been trained in the military to -- to all this kind of vehicle, knew the number of the vehicles, which kind, and which brigade they belong to and all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to your own military training, was there any specific department that you operated in, in the Danish army itself?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, I have been in the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Service, yes. The intelligence -- it's what you call it, the local intelligence. It's on the ground in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it's intelligence unit within an army context?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what exactly did the intelligence element of the Danish army concentrate on or focus on, in general terms, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Not specific, just the kind of thing, the equipment we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We -- we were -- we were not asked to, but some of us took pictures of these cars so we can have them for our own -- you can call it education at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you were travelling through various areas, whether they're JNA or whether they are -- I will call Croatian --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- is it right you had a level of expertise and also an interest in trying to ascertain the -- the weaponry that existed?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on then, if we may, please. You have said that you didn't see any mortars or artillery positions. Can we deal if there was any cease-fire that had been imposed for this -- for this mission? If we look at the fourth entry.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I did not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, if you go to page 6962, the one we have been on.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you look for the fourth entry down, fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you like to just read that particular entry, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: "Local" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Local -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you pause a moment, please. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I am truly sorry interrupting my learned friend. I would like to me one thing though. Is the witness being asked to say what he remembers about his mission, or is he being asked to comment on a report produced by somebody else? I think the right thing to do would be to ask the witness first to give us his own recollections. And after that to possibly comment on reports written by somebody else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Vasic, it's neither of the alternatives you're contemplating. It's the witness giving evidence of his recollection reminded by these notes that were made at the time. Is that right, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is correct. It's a memory-refreshing document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of preliminary questions might have been helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just to know. It's emerged slowly, but basically that these are notes prepared at the time not by him, but by his team leader, that he was familiar with them and they, as he understood, were correct at the time would have overcome the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I apologise for that. I should have done it. If you would like me to do, I'm quite happy to do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Schou, this document you have seen before?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because you have signed it. And clearly it relates to the mission that you were involved in to Vukovar and Vukovar and return?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to the document, you have read it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And would it be right to say that, having read it, that you agree with the contents of the document as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I agree with the contents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And would you wish to refer to this document to assist your memory or recollection? As what we will call an aide-memoire?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, it's an -- that's the way I can -- because it's so long time ago, so I have to -- to be -- to have my papers to see -- to see in front of me what's happened at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I hope that satisfied my learned friends. Can we just deal then, please, with this paragraph starting with: "The local commander informs team V that cease-fire was to be imposed from" -- what time was it, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was from the morning, at 0500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. On what date? The 19th of October, I think?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Until the 21 on 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was it 21 or is it midnight?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you explain, please, the next entry? Can you read it out and then explain it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it. "This is not in accordance with Zagreb-initiated cease-fire agreement which was to be in effect between 700 [sic] hours on Friday, October the 18th and" -- something about the 2400 hours, October the 20th, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just see if maybe my copy is slightly better than yours. Is it between 1700 hours, as opposed to 700 hours? 1-7?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, on Friday, October the 18th. And 2400 hours, i.e., midnight, on October the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The 20th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And when you were in this convoy, did you hear various sounds?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. I think -- no, I'm not sure. The team V, I'm not sure that it is in the convoy. It could be a connection with a team that's in Croatia or something like that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's deal with your recollection, then, if we may. So there you are, you are in the convoy. What happens then next, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Then next we were -- we were escorted -- not escorted but there was a civilian car with four Croats in front of the -- in front of our vehicle, and we travelling through a cornfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: And reach Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: -- from -- from east, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a technical issue. The interpreter trying to do the B/C/S interpretation is really on the edge. The interpretation is getting more and more precarious, I think on account of the pace of the proceedings. If everyone could please just slow down, so that the B/C/S interpretation may again become possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. It's a useful reminder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So let's deal, please, with the arrival at Vukovar itself using your memory. Now, when you got to Vukovar, did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We go strictly to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you remember approximately when it was you went to the hospital? Approximately what time of day?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: 10.00, 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you remember how many other ECM monitors there were with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I think eight. Eight or nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you describe to the Court, please, the actual -- if there was any damage to the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: There were -- there were a lot of damage to the hospital. It was only the basement that were able to take patient and where they have to work. From the -- the -- all the other part of the building, they were totally destroyed. I was taken around with a medical doctor from the hospital, and we could only go through I think it was the second floor because of damage to stairs. And there were no people except in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us whether the hospital itself was marked in any way to demonstrate that it was a hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. The hospital were marked with a red cross on the -- on the -- on the roof, and a red cross on the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you say "a red cross on the field," in my language would you mean on the grass?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: On the grass, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how -- was that grass with -- inside the hospital perimeter or outside?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was in the middle of the hospital. I think the hospital was three buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And how large were these red cross signs?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: On the roof I think it was 10 point -- 10 metre on one side and 10 metre on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you had an opportunity, presumably, of being able to assess the professional or the circumstances in which the medical staff were operating?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, the level of medical supplies that existed at that time within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: They only have few medical stuff to work with. They have to clean again and again. They use the bandage more than one time and then they wash it and take it again and use it again. They have only a small table with medicine, I think 10 or 12 different kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the -- the medical staff themselves, were you able to assess the level of their capabilities or competence?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I did not see them work, but I saw the patient and they were treated well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you look through the hospital comprehensively or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Comprehensively means - my fault - did you look through the hospital thoroughly?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Or did you just go to one part?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. The whole -- the whole hospital -- we went through the whole hospital, yes. And I was escorted -- not escorted but I was shown around from this female doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with whether you saw what I will call military personnel. Did you see military personnel inside the hospital itself with weapons?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. I saw military personnel outside the hospital. You can -- yes, on the ground, but inside the hospital area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: But not in the house [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And -- inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it's right to say that you did hear mortar fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the mortar fire, you didn't see mortars being fired; is that equally right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't see it, but I hear mortaring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Right. How far away would you have assessed the mortar fire was? Sometimes difficult to assess.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: 30, 40 metres, I think. Maybe 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we deal then, please, with the -- the brief itself. What was the purpose of the mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The purpose of the mission was -- were to bring not all the patient but the most of the patient out of the hospital to -- back to a hospital in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to that, how many patients did you actually remove?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I think it was 109 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I deal with the age of the -- the injured persons? And I deal principally with men or males, all right? Was there any guide-lines for taking male patients away --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: There were no guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what about age?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: There were no -- we have no guide-lines about which -- what kind of wounded we had to take away. And it was up to Medecins sans Frontieres and the Croats to decide who would be transportable, or who would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any concern that if the convoy was to be going back through obviously Croat lines but also JNA lines, that the -- the convoy would be stopped and examined by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We know that we had to cross the JNA lines, so we know that of course the convoy will be checked again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was there any concern that men of fighting age might encounter difficulties going through those lines?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I have not heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this might be a leading question. I think it would be proper to ask the witness about these concerns but not lead him on the nature of these concerns, especially having in mind the witness's previous answer, that they had received no instructions in relation to the patients' age or gender, and that in actual fact the Croatian side and the Medecins sans Frontieres were in charge of that aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, thank you for your concern. I think, in the circumstances, given that we're dealing with the 19th of October, given the general tenor of the evidence, that the form of question is not offensive. Carry on, please, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with the -- the people that you removed from the hospital itself? Can you approximate the number of people that were taken out from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, 109, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were they male, female, can you give us an idea of their make-up?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: They were mostly females and they were mostly old men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we deal then, please, with the removal from the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the route. Now, if we go back to your diagram, if you remember it. That's at, as I say, page 6971 at tab 38.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We can see the diagram. Now, with regard to it, the diagram itself, what then happened when you were leaving? Can you just, in general terms, tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yeah. When we leave the hospital, we were crossing a little river, and then -- at that time we were on the normal road, and then we crossed the river and went back the same way we went into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was that across a field?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That was across a field, yes. But on a -- you call it -- on a track or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I would call a farm track?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, a farm track.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. So with regard to that track itself, who was your guide across that track?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Our guide were the Croat -- this civilian car with four Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were travelling out from Vukovar, was there anything that occurred that stopped you going along that farm track?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. In -- just in the beginning of the farm track there was a wire crossing the road, and the wire was not there when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So by that are you saying that it was the same route that you had travelled in?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's the same route we have travelling in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, let us deal with the wire. What do you mean by a wire? Wire can mean many things in English.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. What do you call it, an iron wire across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: A metal wire?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: A metal wire, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you know whether that metal wire was attached to anything?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was -- there were -- in fact there were two wires. The first one the Croatian cut. I don't know nothing else because I was not exactly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. When you say "cut," normally if you cut a trip-wire with an explosive at the end it has an unfortunate effect.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know if this was done in a special way or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let us -- you carried on after you went through that wire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what then happened?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Then there was another wire. And it was also cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On the same route?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: On the same route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And when they were cut, were there any detonations?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So what then happened when you went through the second wire on the same route back?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: After the second wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Then we were driving on this farm -- farmer road, you have said, and suddenly there came in tank in front of us, a JNA tank and a APC, and they pointed out that our car -- I was in the first -- in the first car in the leading car --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: -- at that time, and the civilian car in front with the Croatian, they drive out and disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you just explain that little more fully?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that we were -- we were driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: In front of us there was a civilian car with four Croat soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: And as soon as this tank arrive, they drive in the cornfield and disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the Croat vehicle drove straight into the cornfield and disappeared?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Well, what about you? You're still on the track?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We're still on the track, and we, all four in the car, jump out of the car while it was running.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the -- the Croats or you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Not the Croats. In our car --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: -- in the ECMM car, the driver and the three ECMM members in the car, we jumped out of the car and you can say -- sorry. You can say that we jump into the side of the road so we were not -- so that the tanks couldn't firing at the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I see. So you jumped out of the vehicle because you thought you might be fired on?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well -- and the car kept driving and crashed. Did you see any JNA soldiers at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No, we only saw the tank and the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And after that did you see anybody?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. They -- they come down with the APC and the tanks and you can say arrested us or take us up to a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us whether in actual fact any of those JNA soldiers were officers or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, they were, especially one officer I saw, and it was Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how do you know that the officer that you saw was what you call Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Because I have seen him there, and I saw him later in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you able to assess, you had been in the military, but were you able to assess his rank or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. Normally I would say -- I would say that I can see which kind of rank they have. And at that time I think he was -- he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what about the -- the uniform he was wearing? Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a camouflage uniform, quite new one. You see, normally when you see soldiers in the field you see they have dirty uniforms. Not dirty but of course there would be some dirt on it, but he had quite new uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you have any dealings with the gentleman you considered to be Mr. Sljivancanin? Did you speak to him or he speak to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No, I -- not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, what about himself? Was he with anyone, apart from JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: He was together with some other JNA soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I just deal then, please, with what happened with Major Sljivancanin. Did he speak to you or to your group?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not saying that he speak to our group, he speak more or less to the press. He had arranged a press conference at the top of the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to ask you about. I've asked you about other people. Where did these press people come from?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We were told that they came from the Belgrade TV and I know there was an international TV too. I did not know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. So can we just go back then, please, to what we were talking about? There you are, you've got a tank in front of you, you jump out, and you then are met by, as you consider, Mr. Sljivancanin and some JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And TV, or the press --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The press, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- Is the phrase. "Press" can mean newspapers and press can mean television.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, where were they located, how far away were they when you saw them? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Approximately 30 metres or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you hear Major Sljivancanin speak to the television crews?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. I -- I only saw that he was speaking. I was not allowed to -- I was not at that point that I could hear it. I was together with the other ECMM members, and -- and the -- the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, do you know what language he was speaking in?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you subsequently find out what was being suggested?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the leader of our -- of the team, the ECMM members, leader of the -- he was at that conference or what you call it, with -- at the top of the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: And -- and it was about that we were not following the agreement of the road to Vukovar, that we have to -- that we should have come to Vukovar through this road, through the normal road that passed the hill 120 -- 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, why was it you had not taken the route that had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We were -- it was because the route -- we were told by the Croatian that the route was mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we deal then, please, with the suggestion that you have taken the wrong route. Was there any discussion then about what route you should now take after having been stopped by the tank?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, we were told to take the -- the -- the agreed route back to Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so can we deal then, please, in very general terms, what route you took, or why you took a particular route?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We were told by Major Sljivancanin, or colonel, I think, at that moment, that -- that we should take the route back to Bogdanovci with -- which was in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you shown the route?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. We were shown this way and you have to take this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who told you to take that route?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Major -- Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So when you took the route was that the whole ECMM convoy?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, it was the whole convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can you tell us then, please, what happened when you went down the route that you had been directed to go by Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we -- we had -- were told from the Croatian that there were mines, so of course we were looking for mines when we were driving out of route. I was in the front car together with the leader of the -- of the mission. And we have travelling I think one kilometre or two, then the truck which was number four in the convoy hit a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that was on the route that you had been told to go on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That was on the route we were told to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I deal, please, with hitting a mine. Was anyone injured?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. The -- there were two nurses from the Medecins sans Frontieres which were throwing out the car and were laying on the ground. And at that moment I went back and tried to treat them, so what happened else, I was -- I was -- tried to treat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: Why did you go down a route, the route that was directed by Major Sljivancanin, if you had been told there were mines on it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Because it was the only way we could get out. We have no -- we have no other way to go. And we have -- of course we have 109 wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I deal with the -- the convoy itself then. How did you manage to get out of that particular situation? What route did you take? Well, here you are, you're going on a route, a mine goes off.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, then we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you keep going on that route?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. Then we pull back all the cars and left the cars that were blowing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We of course transferred the wounded from the truck to another truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: And then we went back to the hill where we claimed that the route was mined that we had only wounded, that we had no weapon at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: And then the JNA took us through the fields, and it was through the fields, to another road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you went through the fields, was that the same route that you had taken with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. No. We went more or less through the -- through the city -- I think it's Petrovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's in the other direction. And you can say it's through the front line of the JNA. There were -- there were normally front line with tanks --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: -- moving on the ground and APC and normal civilian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question that I really have is this: Here you are, you have been told to go down a route by the JNA. Clearly there is an explosion from a mine. You go back, you tell the JNA that you've hit mines and really you've only injured people on board. Who did you tell that you had hit a mine? Was Sljivancanin still there or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I don't know. I was working with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I see. Now, the route that you took out, the safe route --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- how close was that to the location that you had been where in actual fact you had hit the mine?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I'm not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. You have a road that's mined.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've been told to go down that route.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you were told to go down another route by the JNA, so it suggests that the JNA have two routes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, but the last route we were suggested to take, it was about 90 degrees to the road, through the fields with normal civilian trucks. So in that field, we get stuck because we couldn't drive there. So we have the APC from the JNA army took us up to -- up through the normal road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Now, the convoy itself, was it ever searched?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who searched it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The -- the Serbian force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when was it searched, in general terms. I don't need --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was searched on the hill first when we meet the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were all the vehicles searched as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, all vehicle were searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what were the JNA looking for? Did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Don't know. No. They didn't tell me. I think -- I'm not sure, but of course they would look for weapon -- weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think then it's right to say that you eventually managed to extricate, to get out from that particular area, and where did you eventually go with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: With the convoy we went to the -- you can say the main road, the highway between Zagreb and Belgrade. And that way we went up to Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then is it right that you were able to deliver the patients in Vinkovci. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was in Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then the ECMM monitors then returned to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: To Zagreb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with -- I may play a video in relation to that, but much, much later. But can I deal, please, with your period of service. Here you are, the 19th of October. I think it's right to say that you have had the benefit of going through the documents from a bundle with a number of tabs on it.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's equally right to say that as far as you can ascertain, the first dealings that you have in relation to this case as far as you can see, is approximately the 19th of November. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with the 19th of November, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to go to a bundle of photographs. They're at divider 41. And if I may deal with it just before my file falls apart. They are 65 ter, number 66. Now, have you got them there at tab 41? Are we able to produce the photographs? We have given the index to the registry. I will repeat it again, 0036-6973 to 00 -- 7002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, we'll have a break now. And in the break, between your case manager and the court officer, we might be able to find what it is that you're wanting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the number that's on the 65 ter list. I've got it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, but it produces what is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we'll see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which, I gather, isn't what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the first morning break now and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm glad to say that on this occasion we were able to help the registry, rather than they help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just deal, please, then, with -- it is, as we have it, tab 41. And there are two photographs. The first -- now, this particular photograph, do you recognise anyone in it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Major Sljivancanin, and I recognise the leader of the Vukovar relief convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know what date this was?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. It was before I arrived Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know where this photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour have a -- the video shown? The photograph shown? I saw Your Honour was -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know when this photograph was actually taken?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I then move on, please, to the photograph, the number is 0036-6977? Now, have you got that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And do you know what this photograph is about?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, it's about the truck that hit the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is that the first vehicle that -- that struck the mine?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's the -- it's number four vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. But the first vehicle that struck -- that hit a mine.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I think the first truck, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I put in both these photographs in respect -- as an exhibit, please? Perhaps they can go in as one -- one exhibit rather than two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received together as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be Exhibit 338.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I deal, as I say, with November the 19th? Because on that occasion you were involved, were you not, with a convoy to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: On the 19th November?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, that's the next Vukovar convoy. This is the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but I want to move on in time. So can we deal then, please, with the formation of that particular convoy, and I want to deal, if I may, please, with the 18th of November. And I'd like you to look at what we will call tab 23. And that is 00381412, 1413. Now, have you got that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It should have a handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Saying "Visit of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal with that, please? The date is the 18th of November. If we look at the composition of the team, we have got Brodin, Kypr, van der Gaag, and Jan Schou, clearly yourself?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's team 1. And then team 2. Now, can you tell us, please, about the schedule that was to be undertaken?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. At the 18th November in the morning we had a meeting in 1st Military District in Belgrade to get access to go to Vukovar area. And we went to a -- to a small city outside Sid where we were stopped, I think, by the -- we were stopped by the JNA. I think it was a check-point or something like that. And we were delayed there about two or three hours, and we had a liaison officer with us from the military district, and he went to -- to Negoslavci to try to get the permission that we could go through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Now, may I just deal with the handwritten document, which you've got in front of you. The numbers are -- you'll see on the bottom right, 1412, and then 1413. Now, with regard to this document, it's -- I think it's not in your handwriting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's not in my handwriting, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But is it right that you have seen this particular document?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I have seen it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: -- here, but I'm not sure I saw it when I were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I know you've seen it here, but you have had a chance to read it. Is it correct that it is a document that agrees with your memory or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It agrees with my memory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you wish to refer to this document to assist your memory if it becomes necessary?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to just move on, then, to the document that just comes after that. Number is 1415 which, actually, in sequence is before 1414, and then there is a map, and the translation is as, my learned friends know, and I think is on the -- on the screen. Now, can we look at the typed document, please, which has an ERN number which is back to front. 1415, it refers to the monitoring activity, 19th of November. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in relation to that document, is it right, I think you have had a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not all of it relates to this particular case, because it deals with Split, Sarajevo and other places, but the first part, the summary, does relate to Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's deal then, please, if we may, and we'll move on to another document in a few moments. Dealing with the 18th of November, what exactly was the brief for the ECMM mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The brief for the members, it was to -- to find out which way we could evacuate or which way the wounded from the hospital could be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we just deal, please, with the handwritten document, we've got number 2, the time schedule.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's work on that. It seems that you departed from the 1st Military District at 0800 hours, 8.00 in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning. I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that a nine?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. You then arrived at Negoslavci at 12.15?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why was there a delay at the check-point en route?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: There was a delay due to the JNA check-point. They did not know we were coming and they -- even if -- even we have this -- we have some papers from the general in -- in Belgrade, we were not allowed to go through the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: And that's why the liaison officer go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, dealing with the briefing in Negoslavci, we've got a briefing at 12.30 and 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember anything about the briefing or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well. After the briefing itself, I think you then went to Vukovar, and that was between 1.50 and 2.30; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what exactly the visit to Vukovar involved?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It -- we went to Vukovar where we saw the -- you can say the front line, we saw from a hill over -- looking out over the city to see, and we were told that there were fighting area in what the map show in the area of 1 and area 2, and there were Croatian soldiers in that area. And -- and area 1 is where the hospital is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were taken to the hill, who took you to the hill?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Now, that hill itself, it was an -- obviously an elevated position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's an elevated position where there were so-called local defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in relation to Major Sljivancanin, when was the first time that you had met him that day?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I think it was at the briefing in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was he present at the briefing?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you remember who it was who actually gave the briefing?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I -- it was -- it was a colonel of the first -- of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal then with the visit itself. Why is it that Major Sljivancanin was with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was because we -- we were, you can say, guarded by the military police, and I think he is a kind of military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told the Court that you saw Major Sljivancanin on the 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Here you are one month later at -- or Vukovar. Did you or did you not recognise him as being the same officer that you had seen earlier on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- of October?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We recognise him and we also ask him why he now were a major, because we think -- we were thinking that the first time he was a colonel. And he -- and he answer that he had always been a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he deny that he was present on the 18th when the explosion had occurred?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he give any level of explanation of what had happened on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Here we are then at the elevated height. Did you actually go to the hospital itself on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No. We could not go to the hospital because of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Then we went to a refugee centre in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the time-schedule itself, can we just look at f, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what have we got there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: We had a -- a briefing in -- in -- in the refugee centre where we were told that the -- the refugees would be taken -- not taken away, but they were going to another -- other parts of Yugoslavia. But when we talk -- we talk with some of the refugees and they said they were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you mean that they said they were told they were not allowed to go? Who had said that they were not allowed to go?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly who persons said that they were not allowed to go, but they said that authority, the military said that they were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to establish what ethnicity were saying that they were not allowed to go?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was because the JNA want them to stay in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but what we're trying to find out is wanting to stay. Are they wanting to Croats to stay, Serbs to stay, Hungarians to stay?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was only Serbs in that refugee centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were told that they -- they had to stay, was any explanation given to you by the JNA about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, please, with the next page. I want to deal with entry (3). Now can you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: You mean the -- okay. "JNA state that every day one or two coaches are bringing them to Sid. A list of those people were required [sic] and will be provided by the next visit."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, if we just look at the top of the page we have got a reference to the town hall. In actual fact, it really should have been c and d, rather than 3 and 4 subbrackets. But anyway, the town hospital and the town hall are situated in zone 1. What was zone 1?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Zone 1 was the -- I think it was the northern part of -- of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we look at page 1415 of the same bundle, we've got a map, have we not? Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I have a map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just acknowledge, so that we have it on the record. We have seem to have two zones. One is marked 1.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the other one is marked 2.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
