utterances.text: Thank you. And then we've got: "Shooting mortar from Vukovar." "The ICRC" -- I'll just read it so it goes into the record -- "bad leader, 2, no help on the 20th, 3, good help 21st." Medecins sans Frontieres, you took the view, doing nothing on the 21st. Dealing with the staff, "left at the first" the first bus?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. It means that the staff of the hospital in Vukovar. They were the first that left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they should have been what?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: They should have been helping loading the people and arrange the people that would be loaded first and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 2, I see a pun. "Very, very God help from the priest."

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No, good -- It means good, good help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps just a slip. So very, very good help from the priest?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The priest and the nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Good work in the hospital, no preparing the evacuation. And then there is reference to the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make application, please, for this exhibit -- this document to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 341.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal, please, with a series of photographs that you took. They have just been referred to, and I don't want to put them all before you but just some. Would you be kind enough, please, to turn up the photographs themselves, and I will give you the various numbers. Have you got 6981? So 0036-6981. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No, not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, that's a different number, isn't it? So 66973. There we are, that's the one we want. Thank you very much. That's kind of you. Now, this photograph, who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Me or one of the other ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know what day this was, 18th, 19th, 20th?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where was it taken?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was taken in the refugee centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we turn over the page, 6983? So it is the next to be shown. Well, second. Yes. This gentleman?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: This gentleman is a Danish EC member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And -- and who was this other fellow?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The other fellow is one of the defenders in the city, one of the Chetniks. And this picture is taken at the hill where we can see the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When this photograph was taken, was there any JNA officer around at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. Just after this photo was taken, Major Sljivancanin came and said we were not allowed to take pictures of the defenders because they were not ordinary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the answer before that said this is one of the defenders, a Chetnik. And I think there is a confusion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The way we use defenders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I put it this way: The way we use "defender" here in this court, we use "defender" invariably to mean a Croatian defender of Vukovar and a chet -- well, I'm trying to just find common ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, please let Mr. Moore finish this and then. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore. No, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have said "defender" and "Chetnik." They tend to mean different things for us.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you be precise?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: I can be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The other person on this picture is a Chetnik who is based inside Vukovar at the hill just -- at the hill we were -- where we were watching the bus station. And he is from -- he is an irregular soldier or what do you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And for clarity, the person in white is the ECMM monitor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's a Danish ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's remove the confusion. Now, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness himself gave the answer. He said it was a defender of the town. It is altogether another matter that those people in the OTP's view were not the defenders of the town. That doesn't necessarily mean they weren't defenders. Maybe that was the impression that the witness had at the time. That can be explained. If that is the witness's answer, this was one of the town's defenders, I don't think there is any reason to change what the witness is saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The confusion, Mr. Borovic, was mine, in that there has been a preponderance of evidence to date that uses the term "defender" in respect of Croatian forces. Now, that means that it is ambiguous as it appeared there, and I felt it necessary to make it clear whether it was Croatian or JNA or Serbian. And we have an answer that makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just move on, and I want to deal with photograph -- there are actually two that I want to be taken in sequence. 0036-6985, firstly, and then followed by 87, please. Could we -- there we are, that's the first one. Again -- thank you. Can we just go back to the first one and then -- that's exactly what I want, but not that one first. The other, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, again, is this one of your photographs?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's one of the ECMM members photographs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's of the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's outside the hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what date was that; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Look to the right-hand side, you see an orange square. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there seems to be two soldiers there. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know who they are or what they are?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we turn over, please, to 87? The next photograph. Thank you very much. Again, the hospital, I want you to look at the roof. Would you be kind enough?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, as we move along the roof to the right-hand side, there seems to be a white square patch?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, that's the rest of the red cross flag on the top of the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the photograph doesn't see the red cross itself. Is that a case it was faded, it didn't exist, or just the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's just the photograph. I saw the red cross on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can I go to the next photograph, which is 89? So 36-6989. This would appear to be as we call the back entrance, the emergency area. What is this? What does this photograph show us, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: This photograph is showing the JNA vehicle in which we are loading the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Patient or patients, plural?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Some of -- I did not -- some of the patient from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I want to take the following photographs in sequence: 91 and 93. 91 and 93. You can show 93 as well, if you would be kind enough. Thank you very much. Now, can you tell us where these photographs were taken, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: They were taken in the front side of the hospital, and it -- I think it -- or I could see some of the hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you remember what day that was?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That was on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to move on to photograph 95, so it's 995. And 999. 995 should be a -- the photographs, people are -- in the hospital itself. Can you tell us when these photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: They're taken on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they -- the other photograph, 99?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It was taken in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the -- the 99 is in October?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the 95?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The previously, it was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then finally, for these photographs, if we go to 997. What exactly is this then, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: This is taken in October, and it is -- it is exactly all the equipment, all the medicine they have in the hospital in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have told us about the -- the convoy leaving on the 20th. And I think it's right to say that you brought to the Tribunal a document, a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that particular document, would you be kind enough, please, to turn up tab 42?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I formally apply for the photographs to be an exhibit, or should I say included in the exhibit where the photographs are mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be included in the Exhibit 338.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to just deal with this document, which I saw for the first time last night at about 6.30, I think. The date is the 21st of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can you just tell us what the headline says? I'm not going ask you to translate the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: The headline is that -- this is, you can say, the dead hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how was it that this particular -- is it on the -- is it on the screen? Yes, we will produce it through Sanction, if we may, with the Court's leave. Now, how was it that this particular article came to be written? What part did you play in the material that's included here?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: On the night -- the night of the 20th -- 20 of November, when I were in the hospital in Sremska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mitrovica, yes?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Mitrovica, I called a Danish newspaper person who were in Belgrade at that time, and I tell her that I have been at -- in the hospital in Vukovar and that I have seen that almost all the men were taken away -- not taken away, but they were not in the hospital when I arrived at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it right that in this document there is reference to that part of your evidence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- it say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read out, if you are able to do so, the short passage that refers to that part of your evidence? Now, where can we find it, first of all? There are three columns.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think you located it last night.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but this is a bad copy, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got the original?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic [sic]. It's Mr. Lukic, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back to where we first began, if the witness will now read something that we're not familiar with, and we don't even have an official interpretation in a language that we understand. We, or our clients, for that matter. Well, my understanding was the witness may be asked something about that conversation but not read out portions of an article that we have never seen before. We have no idea what this is about. Will the witness be translating for us, will he be reading out portions for us? But that is not the gist of his testimony. The gist is he talked to a journalist. Maybe he can tell us something about that, instead of reading an article for our benefit that we have never seen before. I think the Defence is definitely disadvantaged here because we are hardly in a position to ask questions about such a document, a document that is being introduced through the back door, as it were, by the OTP. The witness will now apparently be reading portions of a document that we know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no back door in this courtroom, Mr. Lukic. Understand that. The document comes in the -- at the stage of the witness's evidence where he has told you what he saw on the 20th of November. Rightly or wrongly, that is his evidence. He says confirmation to me and for my evidence that I saw it on the 20th of November, is that I also spoke that day to a reporter and that reporter published an article the next day which mentioned that fact. Now, that's the sole relevance and basis for this document. It enables, when we're looking back 15 years or so, to have another cross-reference on time to the evidence that the witness has expressly given as to what he saw and observed. Now, the witness is about to read in English the Danish newspaper article which will provide us all for the first time with some approximate interpretation. Given the subject matter, it may be unlikely that in the end there will be any dispute, once the members of the Defence have had an opportunity to verify, that there will be any dispute that such an article was published in that newspaper on that day. If that is not a matter of dispute in the end, it will be possible today or tomorrow for the Defence to deal with the simple proposition, "I spoke to a reporter on the 20th and that reporter published an article on the 21st in Denmark." So, on that basis, Mr. Moore may proceed with what is happening, leaving open to Defence full opportunity to test the proposition that this article was ever published. The article itself will not be received in evidence, even if it's tendered, unless the Defence want it. It can be marked for identification. Carry on, please, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have got three columns. Have you got one that you can read now?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the part -- I don't want the whole article read.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: No, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it first, second or third column?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: It's in the middle column. You can see in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, would you be kind enough to read out slowly, please --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- or give us your interpretation of what is written?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: Yes. "Soldiers throw the Red Cross people out and take away a lot of human patient before army evacuate the rest of the hospital of 407 wounded and ill."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Having the added benefit of a Scandinavian speaker with me, the word you translated as "human" I am told may have another meaning. What was the meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was meaning that it was only men that were taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Thelin tells me the word is "male."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Male, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say you then concluded your mission with the evacuation of people from Vukovar on the 20th and 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that for that to be marked for identification. I don't know if it's going to become necessary or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's important for the purposes of the Defence that it be kept on record in case it is disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that concludes --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 342 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I hope you will keep in mind the plea that came from the heart of Mr. Lukic when he commenced his cross-examination of the last witness. That he is always left until last and never has enough time. So that out of sympathy for your colleague, if you can please concentrate on what is important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will certainly keep that in mind, both the witness's testimony and my learned friend's remark. I think it would be a wise idea to perhaps apply the method that has so far proved very useful, perhaps to finish early today so that the Defence teams may be allowed time to better organise ourselves for tomorrow and be more effective. Unfortunately, I had the dubious honour with the last witness to tender a lot of documents, and that's why it took so long. There were tab numbers missing in some cases in some of the documents my learned friend used after me. Be that as it may, I will keep the limitations in mind with this witness, and we shall make it as brief as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's hardly firm enough to give the Chamber enough comfort, "as brief as necessary." It is very clear that the doctor ought to be able to be finished in his evidence tomorrow and away for the weekend. Now, Mr. Lukic has some particular interest with this witness, I would think, so that yourself and Mr. Borovic might approach your questioning accordingly. It's a full quarter of an hour we would be losing. You feel that that will be time well invested?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do believe so. I am quite certain that both my learned friend Borovic and I can do a good job dividing our questions up, thus leafing more than sufficient time for Mr. Lukic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your conversations because he will want some time. Mr. Lukic, you are on your feet for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm a little concerned by the fact that you have just mentioned, Your Honour, that we have to finish the witness tomorrow. So far Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence has always done its best in terms of the needs of any particular witness. We have been very cooperative, I should say. If we are expected tomorrow to comply with certain dead-lines, we might not be able to meet them, especially if there is likely to be any re-examination by Mr. Moore. I can't guarantee that, it's as simple as that. I cannot offer a full guarantee. This is, after all, an exceptionally important witness for us, and we wish to take full advantage of our rights under Article 21. You have pointed out the importance of cross-examination yourself on a number of different occasions. We need to be given a chance to cross-examine effectively without having to look at the clock all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I know the load has fallen on you somewhat unevenly in this respect. And that's why I am urging your two learned colleagues to look very carefully at what they're doing. I think you will also agree that the Chamber has been concerned throughout to enable fair time to all accused and to the Prosecution. We have not imposed arbitrary time limits on anybody. But increasingly, and consistently, witnesses are taking much longer than anticipated, and the trial is slipping out longer and longer. And if you look back over the record, so much time has been spent on issues that are side issues. There aren't many critical issues in this case, they are critical and they deserve full attention, but so many of the issues that are not critical have absorbed a lot of time, and I, in that observation, include all counsel, Prosecution and Defence. The Chamber will increasingly have to become insistent on time limits, because we cannot allow the trial to keep dragging longer without good reason. If there's good reason, I think you see already that we do not limit. But when we don't see good reason we're just going to have to be more determined, because this trial must finish, in fairness to your clients, in fairness to the other accused waiting for their trials to begin. So, with those words of encouragement, we ask Defence counsel to look tonight. It's also fair enough to say that the witness would be here over a weekend and would have to wait into next week if it was not finished tomorrow. So bear that in mind. We will adjourn now and be ready for one of the very good performances tomorrow of all counsel as they focus on the important issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
